theory.intro: A surd is in **simplest form** when the number under the root has no square factor left. Once every surd in an expression is simplified, the four operations behave exactly like they do with pronumerals: $5\sqrt{3}-2\sqrt{3}=3\sqrt{3}$ works the same way as $5x-2x=3x$.
facts: To simplify a surd, factorise the radicand using its **highest square factor**, then split it: $\sqrt{72}=\sqrt{36}\times\sqrt{2}=6\sqrt{2}$.
Only **like surds** — those with the same radicand — can be added or subtracted: $4\sqrt{5}+3\sqrt{5}=7\sqrt{5}$, but $4\sqrt{5}+3\sqrt{2}$ cannot be collected.
To multiply, multiply coefficients and radicands separately: $a\sqrt{x}\times b\sqrt{y}=ab\sqrt{xy}$.
To divide, divide coefficients and radicands separately: $a\sqrt{x}\div b\sqrt{y}=\dfrac{a}{b}\sqrt{\dfrac{x}{y}}$.
Always check the final surd: $2\sqrt{50}$ is not finished, because $\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt{2}$ gives $10\sqrt{2}$.
